sections.label: What it is
sections.body: Answer the actual question immediately before giving background, qualifications, or explanations.

sections.label: Why use it
sections.body: It makes the response relevant from the beginning, reduces unnecessary hesitation, and prevents students from sounding rehearsed.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: Q: Do you enjoy cooking? Weak: "Well, there are many different factors that I would consider when talking about cooking..." Better: "Yes, I do. I especially enjoy cooking when I have enough time to experiment."

sections.label: When to use
sections.body: Part 1, and as a general habit in Parts 2–3 whenever an answer needs a clear position.

sections.label: Common mistake
sections.body: Turning the technique into a formula such as "Firstly, I would like to say..." Natural conversation starts naturally.

sections.label: Practice
sections.body: Answer ten Part 1 questions. The first sentence must directly answer the question. Then develop the answer naturally.

sections.label: What it is
sections.body: A flexible Part 1 development framework.

sections.label: Answer
sections.body: Give your position immediately.

sections.label: Reason
sections.body: Explain why.

sections.label: Example / Elaboration
sections.body: Add a concrete detail, brief example, contrast, personal experience, or consequence.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: Q: Do you like living where you are? A: "Yes, I do. It's mainly because it's fairly quiet and most places I need are within walking distance. I can get to shops and cafés without having to use a car."

sections.label: Important
sections.body: A.R.E. is a scaffold, not a mandatory three-sentence template. Some questions only need an answer and a reason. Some naturally develop through contrast rather than an example.

sections.label: Avoid
sections.body: Making every Part 1 answer the same length or structure.

sections.label: Practice
sections.body: Give one 10-second answer, then expand it naturally to 20 seconds without adding irrelevant information.

sections.label: What it is
sections.body: After giving an answer, ask yourself "Why?" and provide one meaningful reason.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: Q: Do you enjoy reading? A: "Yes, especially non-fiction, because I like learning about subjects that I wouldn't normally encounter in everyday life."

sections.label: Why it works
sections.body: Many short answers fail simply because the student stops after the first statement.

sections.label: Avoid
sections.body: Adding three or four weak reasons merely to make the answer longer.

sections.label: Practice
sections.body: Take 20 Part 1 questions and answer each with one clear reason.

sections.label: What it is
sections.body: Replace vague language with precise language.

sections.label: Weak
sections.body: "It was a good place."

sections.label: Better
sections.body: "It was a surprisingly peaceful place with very little traffic."

sections.label: Weak
sections.body: "I like technology."

sections.label: Better
sections.body: "I like technology that saves me repetitive work."

sections.label: Ask
sections.body: What exactly do I mean by "good", "bad", "interesting", "important", "nice", or "thing"?

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.body: Precision is more useful than forcing rare vocabulary.

sections.label: Practice
sections.body: Record a short answer. Circle every vague word. Retry using a more precise expression.

sections.label: What it is
sections.body: Add natural contrast to make an answer more nuanced.

sections.label: Useful patterns
sections.body: "I generally..., although..." "I used to..., but now..." "Usually..., whereas..." "On the one hand..., but..."

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "I usually study alone because I concentrate better that way, although I enjoy group study when we are working on a creative project."

sections.label: Use it when
sections.body: The answer is too simple and a natural contrast exists.

sections.label: Do not
sections.body: Invent a contrast just to sound advanced.

sections.label: What it is
sections.body: Move from a personal or concrete example to a broader observation.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "In my own experience, online classes are convenient because I can study from anywhere. More broadly, that flexibility probably explains why online education has become attractive to working adults."

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.body: This is especially useful in Part 3, where students need to move beyond purely personal answers.

sections.label: Recommended structure
sections.body: Context → Core event → Turning point → Outcome → Reflection.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "I first met this person when I was at school. At that time I wasn't particularly confident about public speaking. One day, she encouraged me to enter a speaking competition. I nearly changed my mind, but I eventually took part. I didn't win, but the experience changed how I thought about public speaking."

sections.label: Why it works
sections.body: A story gives the student a natural source of continuous language instead of treating the cue-card bullets as four unrelated questions.

sections.label: Use with
sections.body: Keywords, not full sentences.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: During the one-minute preparation period, write memory triggers rather than sentences.

sections.label: Good
sections.body: "summer / cousin / mountains / rain / lost phone / restaurant / relieved"

sections.label: Bad
sections.body: "I went to the mountains with my cousin last summer and while we were there..." A keyword should trigger a chunk of meaning.

sections.label: Suggested map
sections.body: WHEN / WHERE WHO WHAT TURNING POINT FEELING WHY IT MATTERED

sections.label: Goal
sections.body: Use the notes to remember content, not to read a speech.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: When a Part 2 answer becomes a list of events, add meaning.

sections.label: Useful questions
sections.body: How did you feel? Why did it matter? What surprised you? What changed afterward? What do you remember most? Would you do it again?

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "The trip itself wasn't particularly unusual. What made it memorable was that I had been under a lot of pressure at the time, so spending the day with my family helped me clear my head." This adds depth without requiring extraordinary vocabulary.

sections.label: When a Part 2 answer starts running out of content, mentally ask
sections.body: "What happened next?"

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "We arrived at the restaurant..." "What happened next?" "We realized that we had booked the wrong branch..." "What happened next?" "Instead of leaving, we decided to stay..." This creates chronological development naturally.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Use when a topic can naturally be discussed across time.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "I first became interested in photography three years ago. These days I mainly take photos when I travel. In the future, I'd like to learn more about portrait photography." Do not force this onto topics where the time shift feels artificial.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Use primarily as a Part 3 thinking scaffold.

sections.label: Point
sections.body: State a position.

sections.label: Explanation
sections.body: Explain why.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: Give a concrete or hypothetical example.

sections.label: Perspective
sections.body: Qualify the claim, consider another side, or explain an exception.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "Governments should invest more in public transport. The main reason is that better transport can reduce congestion and make commuting more predictable. For example, a reliable metro system can move large numbers of people without adding more cars to the roads. That said, the priorities are different in sparsely populated areas where public transport may be less practical."

sections.label: Important
sections.body: Do not make every response visibly follow four steps.

sections.label: When a Part 3 idea is underdeveloped
sections.body: Why is it true? How does it happen? Can I give an example?

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "Social media can influence opinions because people are repeatedly exposed to similar information. Recommendation systems can reinforce the same type of content, so users may gradually see fewer opposing views. For example, someone who repeatedly watches one type of political content may receive increasingly similar recommendations."

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Useful for "why" and "what effects" questions.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "People move to cities because there are more employment opportunities. This attracts a younger workforce, which increases demand for housing. As a result, rents may rise and competition for accommodation can become stronger." The middle step is important. Do not jump from cause straight to an enormous claim.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: If you cannot generate an idea, change whose perspective you are using.

sections.label: Possible stakeholders
sections.body: individual student parent teacher employer business government local community older generation younger generation Example topic: AI in education Student: "It can personalize learning." Teacher: "It may reduce repetitive administrative work." Government: "It could expand access to educational resources." Employer: "It may increase demand for digital skills." This is one of the fastest ways to escape an idea-generation block.

sections.label: Ask
sections.body: What do we gain? What do we sacrifice? Who benefits? Who bears the cost?

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "Remote work gives employees more flexibility, but companies may find it harder to maintain collaboration and team cohesion."

sections.label: Useful language
sections.body: "While this offers..., it can also..." "The main benefit is..., although the downside is..." "The advantage needs to be weighed against..."

sections.label: A nuanced answer can follow
sections.body: Claim → normal case → exception.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "Online learning is generally more convenient because students can study anywhere. However, that advantage is less significant for subjects that require specialist equipment or direct supervision." Do not stop at "It depends." Say what it depends on.

sections.label: When a Part 3 question feels empty, generate five directions
sections.body: 1. Cause — Why? 2. Effect — What happens because of it? 3. Comparison — Who experiences it differently? 4. Future — What could change? 5. Exception — When would the claim not apply? Example topic: public transport Cause: congestion and limited road space Effect: easier commuting and potentially lower emissions Comparison: large cities vs rural communities Future: increased electrification and automation Exception: low-density areas may need other solutions Use this to generate ideas before searching for advanced vocabulary.

sections.label: Never stop at
sections.body: "It depends."

sections.label: Complete the thought
sections.body: "It depends on the person's financial situation." "It depends on whether you are talking about large cities or rural areas." "It depends on how heavily the system is regulated." This turns a weak hedge into an actual qualification.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: The goal is not zero pauses.

sections.label: Good pause
sections.body: "I think public transport / is particularly important in large cities / because..."

sections.label: Unhelpful pause
sections.body: "I think... um... public... uh... transport... is..." Pause between ideas rather than repeatedly stopping during a single idea.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Speak in meaning groups rather than word-by-word.

sections.label: Instead of
sections.body: "I / think / public / transport / should / be..."

sections.label: Use
sections.body: "I think public transport / should be more heavily subsidized / in major cities." Chunking supports fluency, pronunciation, breathing, and processing.

sections.label: Practice
sections.body: Mark slash boundaries in a sentence. Read it slowly. Then repeat at a natural speed while preserving the meaning groups.

sections.label: Useful bridge phrases
sections.body: "That's an interesting one." "Let me think about that for a second." "I'd say it depends." "I hadn't really thought about it before, but..." "One way of looking at it is..." Use them sparingly.

sections.label: Avoid artificial phrases like
sections.body: "That is an extraordinarily thought-provoking question which requires profound consideration." The purpose is to buy a small amount of thinking time, not to perform sophistication.

sections.label: First identify personal fillers
sections.body: "um", "uh", "basically", "you know", "actually", etc.

sections.label: Then practice replacing some of them with
sections.body: a short silent pause a breath a natural bridge phrase a clearer sentence start Do not attempt to eliminate every natural hesitation.

sections.label: The goal
sections.body: Less disruptive filler, not robotic silence.

sections.label: Basic method
sections.body: 4 minutes → same topic 3 minutes → same topic, more efficient 2 minutes → same topic, most concise

sections.label: IELTS adaptation
sections.body: 2 minutes → 90 seconds → 60 seconds or 3 minutes → 2 minutes → 90 seconds The objective is not speed for its own sake. The objective is reducing unnecessary repetition, filler, and planning delay.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Do not train students to speak as fast as possible.

sections.label: Good speaking has
sections.body: stable pace clear articulation natural pauses enough time for the listener to process information Fast + unclear + rushed is not a useful target.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: When the exact word disappears, continue communicating. If the word "pedestrian crossing" is unavailable: "It's the place where people cross the road safely." If "receipt" is unavailable: "The small piece of paper you get after you pay for something."

sections.label: The principle
sections.body: A missing word should not destroy the entire idea.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: A structured circumlocution method.

sections.label: Category
sections.body: "It's a type of public transport..."

sections.label: Function
sections.body: "It's mainly used for short journeys around cities..."

sections.label: Description
sections.body: "It runs on tracks and usually stops at fixed stations." Then the student may remember the exact word. This should become automatic through practice.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Do not learn vocabulary as isolated words.

sections.label: Instead of
sections.body: "congestion"

sections.label: Learn
sections.body: heavy traffic congestion ease congestion reduce congestion traffic congestion in urban areas

sections.label: Instead of
sections.body: "decision"

sections.label: Learn
sections.body: make a difficult decision reach a decision weigh up a decision a life-changing decision The aim is ready-to-use natural language.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Replace vague words only when the replacement is actually more precise. "good teacher" can become: "supportive teacher" "knowledgeable teacher" "engaging teacher" "patient teacher" Do not replace "good" mechanically with an obscure synonym.

sections.label: Ask
sections.body: "What exactly do I mean?"

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Say the same idea three ways.

sections.label: Original
sections.body: "Online learning is convenient."

sections.label: Version 2
sections.body: "One major advantage of online education is its flexibility."

sections.label: Version 3
sections.body: "Students can access learning materials without being tied to a particular location or timetable." This trains flexibility and retrieval rather than memorization of a single phrase.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Identify the stressed syllable in important words.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: PHOtograph phoTOGraphy

sections.label: Practice
sections.body: 1. identify stress 2. exaggerate the stressed syllable slightly 3. reduce unstressed syllables 4. say the word naturally Do not turn this into an imitation of a specific accent.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Important information should normally receive stronger stress. "I didn't say he stole the money."

sections.label: Changing the stressed word changes the implied contrast
sections.body: "I" / "stole" / "money" Practice by saying one sentence several times with different stressed words and discussing what the listener would infer.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Break long speech into meaningful groups. "I think governments should invest more in public transportation / because traffic is becoming increasingly serious / and people are spending too much time commuting." Train meaning groups, not word-by-word pauses.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Choose 30–120 seconds of natural English.

sections.label: Process
sections.body: 1. Listen once. 2. Listen again with a transcript if available. 3. Speak simultaneously with the speaker. 4. Copy rhythm, pauses, stress, intonation, linking, and timing. 5. Record yourself. 6. Listen back. 7. Retry. Focus on speech features, not on pretending to have the speaker's accent.

sections.label: Answer a question three ways
sections.body: A. natural position B. opposite position C. nuanced / conditional position

sections.label: Example
sections.body: A: "Part-time work can teach students responsibility." B: "I'd discourage it during particularly demanding academic periods." C: "It depends on the student's workload; a few hours can be beneficial, but excessive work can interfere with study." The goal is adaptability.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Take one topic and deliberately change the question. Topic: technology "What technology do you use most?" "How has technology changed education?" "Is technology making people less independent?" "Should children have unrestricted access to technology?" "What will technology look like in twenty years?" This detects whether the student has learned flexible language or memorized one answer.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Give an answer, then defend the opposite. Do not worry about personal belief. The purpose is to strengthen argument flexibility.

sections.label: Procedure
sections.body: 1. State position A. 2. Give a reason and example. 3. Reverse the position. 4. Defend position B. 5. Finish with a nuanced position.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: During fluency practice, allow one minor error without stopping the sentence.

sections.label: Goal
sections.body: Teach the brain that a small error does not require a full restart. After the answer, review the mistake separately.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: Separate communication mode from analysis mode.

sections.label: During speaking
sections.body: Continue communicating.

sections.label: After recording
sections.body: Identify and correct grammar, vocabulary, or pronunciation problems. This is particularly useful for students whose self-monitoring destroys fluency.

sections.label: After every Part 3 answer, mentally ask
sections.body: Why? Can you give an example? What if the opposite happened? Would this always be true? How might the future change this? This prepares the student for spontaneous examiner follow-ups.

sections.label: Useful language
sections.body: "I can see why people think that, but..." "To some extent, I agree, although..." "That may be true in some cases, but..." "I'd qualify that by saying..." The objective is nuanced reasoning, not aggressive disagreement.

sections.label: Use
sections.body: "I can't remember the exact word, but..." "What I mean is..." "It's basically..." "It's something you use to..." "It's a type of..." Then continue. Do not spend several seconds trying to recover a word that has already disappeared.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: "Yesterday I go—went to the..." Then continue.

sections.label: Avoid
sections.body: "Yesterday I go—went—no, I went—actually, I had gone..." One repair is enough unless the original meaning is unclear.

sections.label: Useful bridges
sections.body: "What I mean is..." "Another way of looking at it is..." "More generally..." "One reason for that could be..." Use the idea that remains rather than chasing a sentence you have mentally lost.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: If the question is not understood, clarification is better than answering the wrong question.

sections.label: Useful
sections.body: "Could you repeat that, please?" "Could you rephrase the question?" "What do you mean by...?" The student should ask naturally and then answer the clarified question.

sections.label: Do not think
sections.body: "I have prepared answer number 17."

sections.label: Think
sections.body: "The examiner asked me this specific question."

sections.label: Process
sections.body: listen → identify what changed → answer → listen again → adapt. This is essential for interactive speaking.

sections.label: Overview
sections.body: After a drill, do not immediately ask the exact same question again.

sections.label: Example
sections.body: Target skill = vocabulary retrieval Question 1: technology Question 2: education Question 3: work Question 4: AI If the skill survives changing content, it is becoming automatic.

sections.label: Correct cycle
sections.body: Problem → targeted drill → immediate speaking question → retry → new related question → later retention check Do not stop at reading an explanation. The retry is the evidence that training transferred into speaking.

sections.label: TRY
sections.body: Give an unscripted answer.

sections.label: DISCOVER
sections.body: Identify one concrete failure.

sections.label: PRACTICE
sections.body: Repair exactly that weakness.

sections.label: BUILD
sections.body: Use the same idea three different ways.

sections.label: Try
sections.body: "I think public transport is good because it helps cities."

sections.label: Discover
sections.body: "Good" is vague; second idea was missing; pause before the next sentence.

sections.label: Practice
sections.body: "efficient for congested cities", "reduce traffic pressure", "provide affordable mobility"

sections.label: Build
sections.body: Version 1: economic perspective Version 2: environmental perspective Version 3: commuter convenience perspective The goal is observable improvement, not theoretical understanding.

sections.label: Pronunciation loop
sections.body: Shadow natural speech. Speak independently. Compare your recording.

sections.label: Listen specifically for
sections.body: rhythm stress pausing chunking clarity speed Do not compare accent identity. ============================================================
